unit.title: Interpret and draw standard electrical drawings

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: Which drawing shows where the lights, switches and outlets are placed in a building?
options: A block diagram of the system
A layout drawing (floor plan)
A circuit (schematic) diagram
A component parts list

questions.stem: What does a circuit (schematic) diagram show?
options: The real position of each item on the wall
The route each cable takes through the building
The price and maker of each part in the circuit
How the parts are connected so the circuit works

questions.stem: Which drawing shows each terminal and the actual wire connected to it, as it is really wired?
options: A block diagram
A site plan
A wiring diagram
An elevation drawing

questions.stem: What is a block diagram mainly used for?
options: To show the main parts of a system and how they link
To show the exact length of every cable on the job
To show every screw terminal and its wire colour
To show the position of each outlet to scale

questions.stem: A single-line (one-line) diagram is often used to show a distribution system. What does one line on it stand for?
options: One single conductor only, such as the neutral
One earth conductor running beside the circuit
All the conductors of that circuit together
A cable that has not yet been installed on site

questions.stem: A symbol is a vertical line with three horizontal lines below it, each shorter than the one above. What does it stand for?
options: A fuse in the line conductor
An earth (ground) connection
A battery of several cells
A lamp or indicator light

questions.stem: On a circuit diagram, what does a solid dot where two lines meet or cross mean?
options: The two wires are joined at that point
The two wires cross but are not joined
A fuse is fitted at that point
That point must be tested before the others

questions.stem: Which component may be drawn either as a zigzag line or as a plain rectangle, depending on the symbol set used?
options: A capacitor
A switch
A lamp
A resistor

questions.stem: On a circuit diagram, what does a circle with a cross (X) inside it usually stand for?
options: A motor
A socket outlet
An earth point
A lamp

questions.stem: On a circuit diagram, what does a circle with the letter M inside it stand for?
options: A meter
A motor
A main switch
A microphone

questions.stem: In the symbol for a battery cell, what does the longer, thinner line show?
options: The negative terminal
The earth terminal
The positive terminal
The fuse in the battery

questions.stem: Why does every set of drawings include a legend (key) of symbols?
options: Because symbols can differ between drawings and offices
Because the legend shows the scale of every drawing
Because the law says every drawing must be in colour
Because the legend replaces the need for a title block

questions.stem: A room is drawn at a scale of 1:50. One wall measures 90 mm on the drawing. How long is the real wall?
options: 9 m

questions.stem: A real wall is 6 m long. How long should it be drawn at a scale of 1:100?
options: 60 mm
6 mm
600 mm
100 mm

questions.stem: What does a scale of 1:20 mean?
options: 1 mm on the real job is 20 mm on the drawing
The drawing is 20 times bigger than the real thing
1 mm on the drawing is 20 mm on the real job
The drawing must be printed on 20 sheets of paper

questions.stem: A size is written on a printed drawing. Why should you use the written size rather than measure the print with a rule?
options: Because a steel rule is not accurate enough for drawings
Because printed drawings are always drawn at full size
Because written sizes are only there to help the customer
Because a print may stretch, so the written size is right

questions.stem: Which of these is normally found in the title block of a drawing?
options: The drawing number, scale, date and who drew it
The full list of materials with their prices
The wiring colours for every circuit on the job
The test results for each circuit in the building

questions.stem: A drawing has been changed and is now Revision C. What should happen to the Revision B copies on site?
options: Keep both and use whichever is easier to read
Use Revision B, because it was checked first
Take them out of use or mark them out of date
Give them to the customer to keep for later

questions.stem: On an electrical layout drawing, what is usually shown by a curved dashed line from a switch to a light?
options: The exact route the cable takes through the wall
Which switch controls which light
That the light must be fitted at a later date
The length of cable needed for the light

questions.stem: What is a dimension line used for on a drawing?
options: To show the outline of an object that you can see
To show the centre line through a circle or a hole
To show an edge of the object that is hidden from view
To show the distance between two points

questions.stem: Which pencil grade gives the lightest, hardest line, good for faint guide lines?
options: 2B
HB
B
2H

questions.stem: Which instrument is used along the edge of a drawing board to draw horizontal lines?
options: A T-square
A compass
A protractor
An eraser shield

questions.stem: Which two set squares are usually found in a drawing kit?
options: 90° and 180° only

questions.stem: Which instrument is used to draw a circle?
options: A set square
A scale rule
A compass
A French curve

questions.stem: What size is an A4 sheet of paper?
How does an A3 sheet of paper compare with an A4 sheet?
options: A3 is half the size of A4
A3 is the same size but thicker
A3 is four times the size of A4
A3 is twice the size of A4

questions.stem: In a one-way lighting circuit, in which conductor must the switch be connected?
options: The neutral conductor
The line (live) conductor
The earth conductor
Any of the three conductors

questions.stem: A stair light is switched from both the top and the bottom of the stairs. Which switches are drawn? (A two-way switch is called a "three-way" switch in North American catalogues.)
options: Two two-way switches
Two one-way switches in series
One one-way switch and a fuse
One intermediate switch only

questions.stem: Three switches control one light in a long corridor. Which switches are needed?
options: Two two-way switches and one intermediate switch
Three one-way switches all wired in series together
Three intermediate switches and no others
One two-way switch and two one-way switches in line

questions.stem: A layout drawing shows 6 lights, 4 switches and 10 outlets. How many items are to be fitted in all?
Before you start work from a drawing, what should you check first?
options: That the drawing has been printed in full colour
That the customer has signed and dated every page
That it is drawn by the same person as last time
That it is the right job and the latest revision

questions.stem: A note on the drawing says: "All outlets 300 mm above finished floor level unless shown otherwise." What does this mean?
options: Every outlet must be fitted 300 mm from the ceiling
Outlets may be fitted at any height you choose
Set outlets 300 mm up from the finished floor
Outlets must be 300 mm apart along the wall

questions.stem: What does "FFL" mean on a building drawing?
options: Fire and flood line
Finished floor level
First floor layout
Full fitting length

questions.stem: On an electrical drawing, what does "DB" usually mark?
options: A door bell push button
A data and telephone box
The distribution board
A double bulb light fitting

questions.stem: When you draw a circuit diagram, how should the lines between the symbols be drawn?
options: Straight, horizontal or vertical, with few crossings
Curved, to show the real route of each cable
At any angle, as long as every part is shown
As thick as possible so they show on a photocopy

questions.stem: Why should you draw a light, faint layout first and then line it in darker?
options: To use less lead in the pencil
So the drawing can be finished more quickly
Because dark lines cannot be drawn with a T-square
So mistakes can be rubbed out before lining in

questions.stem: What is the best order for producing a layout drawing of a room?
options: Draw the symbols, then the walls, then the title block
Write the title block, then guess the room size and draw
Draw the walls freehand, then go back and measure the room
Measure the room, draw walls to scale, then add symbols

questions.stem: When is a freehand sketch useful to an electrician?
options: To record a site layout quickly before a proper drawing
To replace the approved drawing for the whole job
To show the inspector instead of the test results
To work out the cost of the job for the customer

questions.stem: How should notes and labels be written on a drawing?
options: In joined-up handwriting, as small as possible
In red ink, so that they stand out on the page
In clear capital letters of an even size
In pencil so faint that they do not spoil the drawing

questions.stem: In which unit are sizes usually written on a metric building drawing?
options: Centimetres
Millimetres
Inches
Metres and feet

questions.stem: How should drawings be looked after on site?
options: Kept dry and clean, flat or rolled, in a set place
Folded up small and kept in your back trouser pocket
Left on the floor where everyone can see them
Pinned outside in the sun and rain all day

questions.stem: Why is a wiring diagram useful when connecting a control panel or a distribution board?
options: It shows how the building looks from the outside
It shows which wire goes to which terminal
It shows the price of each part in the board
It shows where the building's water pipes run

questions.stem: Which component is drawn as two coils side by side, often with straight lines between them?
options: A resistor
A capacitor
A fuse
A transformer

questions.stem: On a circuit diagram, what does a symbol of two parallel lines of equal length, with a small gap between them, stand for?
options: A resistor
A lamp
A capacitor
A switch

questions.stem: On a layout drawing, a light symbol is marked "a" and two switches are also marked "a". What does this tell you?
options: The light and both switches are on different circuits
The light is controlled by a dimmer switch only
The switches control lights in another room
Both switches marked "a" control that light

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: A drawing is at a scale of 1:50. A line on it is 40 mm long. What is the real length, in metres?
At a scale of 1:20, how long, in millimetres, should a 1 m long panel be drawn?
Name the ruler that is marked with several scales, such as 1:50 and 1:100.
Name the instrument used to measure and draw angles on a drawing.
What is the name of the plastic sheet with symbol shapes cut out of it, used to draw symbols neatly?
What is the name of a drawing that shows one wall of a room or building as seen from the front?
What is the name of a view of a building cut straight through from top to bottom to show the inside?
What is the name of the line made of long and short dashes, used to show the centre of a circle?
What is the name of the thin line drawn out from an object, so that a dimension line can be placed between two of them?
On a circuit diagram, which instrument is shown by a circle with the letter V inside it?
Name the protective device that melts and breaks the circuit when too much current flows.
What are the two conductors that link a pair of two-way switches called?
What is the name of the drawing made at the end of a job to show how the work was really installed?
What do the letters NTS mean when they are written on a drawing?
What name is given to the conductor that runs from a switch to the lamp and is live only when the switch is on?

essays.stem: Explain the difference between a layout drawing, a circuit diagram and a wiring diagram, and say what each one is used for.
essays.modelAnswer: A layout drawing, or floor plan, is drawn to scale and shows where the lights, switches, outlets and the distribution board are placed in each room. It is used to mark out positions on site and to count the items needed. A circuit (schematic) diagram uses symbols to show how the parts of a circuit are connected so that it works, for example how a switch controls a lamp. It does not show where the parts are in the building. It is used to understand a circuit and to find faults. A wiring diagram shows each terminal and the actual wire that goes to it, much as it is really wired. It is used when connecting accessories, control panels and distribution boards.
markingPoints: Layout drawing: to scale, shows where items are placed in the building
Circuit diagram: shows how parts connect and work, not where they are
Wiring diagram: shows each terminal and the wire connected to it
Gives a correct use for each drawing

essays.stem: Explain what a scale of 1:50 means. Then show how you would work out the real length of a cable run that measures 120 mm on a 1:50 drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: A scale of 1:50 means that 1 unit on the drawing stands for 50 of the same units in real life. So 1 mm on the drawing is 50 mm on site, and the real building is 50 times bigger than the drawing. A scale lets a large building fit on a sheet of paper while keeping everything in the right proportion. To find the real length, I measure the run on the drawing: 120 mm. Then I multiply by 50: 120 × 50 = 6 000 mm. I change millimetres to metres by dividing by 1 000, so the real run is 6 m. If a size is written on the drawing, I use the written size instead of measuring the print.
markingPoints: 1 unit on the drawing equals 50 of the same units in real life
Says why scales are used
Multiplies correctly: 120 × 50 = 6 000 mm
Converts correctly to 6 m
Uses written dimensions in preference to measuring the print

essays.stem: Describe the information found in the title block and in the legend of an electrical drawing, and say why each one is important.
essays.modelAnswer: The title block is usually in the bottom right-hand corner. It gives the project name and address, the drawing title, the drawing number, the scale, the date, the revision letter, and the names of the people who drew and checked it. It is important because it tells you that you have the right drawing for the job, that it is the latest revision, and which scale to use. The legend, or key, lists each symbol on the drawing and says what it means, such as a lamp, a one-way switch, an outlet or the distribution board. It may also explain abbreviations and line types. It is important because symbols can differ from one office or standard to another, so the legend stops mistakes in reading the drawing.
markingPoints: Title block contents: title, number, scale, date, revision, drawn and checked by
Title block shows it is the right, latest drawing and gives the scale
Legend lists each symbol and its meaning (and abbreviations)
Legend matters because symbols differ between offices and standards

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to produce a layout drawing of a bedroom that has one light, one switch and three outlets.
essays.modelAnswer: First I measure the room with a tape: the length and width, the position and width of the door and window, and the wall thickness. I make a quick freehand sketch and write the sizes on it. Next I choose a scale, such as 1:50, and a paper size, and fix the paper to the board. I draw a border and a title block. Using a scale rule, T-square and set square, I draw the walls lightly, then the door and window. I add the symbols in place: the light near the centre of the ceiling, the switch beside the door on the opening side, and the three outlets where they are needed. I link the switch to the light with a dashed line. I add a legend, notes such as outlet heights, and dimensions. Then I line in, check the drawing and complete the title block.
markingPoints: Measures the room and makes a sketch with sizes
Chooses a scale and paper, and draws a border and title block
Draws walls, door and window lightly to scale with the right instruments
Places correct symbols and shows which switch controls the light
Adds legend, notes and dimensions, lines in and checks

essays.stem: Describe how you would draw the circuit diagram for a lighting circuit in which one one-way switch controls two lamps.
essays.modelAnswer: I start by drawing the supply on the left: the line and neutral from the distribution board, with the circuit breaker or fuse symbol in the line conductor. I draw the line conductor going to one side of the one-way switch symbol. From the other side of the switch, I draw the switched line to the lamps. The two lamps are drawn in parallel, so the switched line goes to both of them, and the neutral comes back from both lamps to the neutral of the supply. I also show the earth conductor going to each lamp point. I use the lamp symbol from the legend, draw the lines straight, horizontal and vertical, put dots where conductors join, and label L, N and E. Finally I add a title and a key.
markingPoints: Shows the supply with the protective device in the line conductor
Places the switch in the line conductor
Draws the two lamps in parallel on the switched line
Returns the neutral from both lamps to the supply; shows earth
Neat conventions: straight lines, junction dots, labels L, N, E, title and key

essays.stem: You are given a drawing for a new job. Describe how you would check and read it before you start work.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the title block. I check the project name, the drawing number and the revision, and I make sure it is the latest issue for this job. I note the scale, and whether any part is marked NTS (not to scale). Next I read the legend to learn the symbols, and I read all the notes, such as mounting heights, cable types and special instructions. I find a known room or the north point so that I can match the drawing to the building. Then I follow each circuit from the distribution board to every point, and count the lights, switches and outlets. I use the written sizes rather than measuring the print. If anything is unclear or does not match the site, I ask my supervisor before I start.
markingPoints: Checks the title block, drawing number and latest revision
Notes the scale and any parts not to scale
Reads the legend and all the notes
Follows each circuit and counts the points; uses written sizes
Asks the supervisor about anything unclear before starting

essays.stem: Describe the drawing equipment needed to produce a neat drawing by hand, and say how to care for it.
essays.modelAnswer: I need a drawing board with a T-square to draw horizontal lines, and two set squares, a 45° one and a 30/60° one, for vertical and sloping lines. A scale rule lets me draw to scale without working out every size. A compass draws circles and arcs, and a protractor measures angles. I use pencils of different grades: a hard 2H for light guide lines, and HB for lining in and for lettering. An eraser, a symbol template and masking tape to hold the paper are also needed. To care for the equipment, I keep the edges of the T-square and set squares clean and free of nicks, never cut along them with a knife, keep pencils sharp, and store everything flat and dry in a case.
markingPoints: Drawing board, T-square and set squares, with what each is for
Scale rule, compass and protractor
Pencil grades: hard for guide lines, HB for lining in
Eraser, template and masking tape
Care: clean, undamaged edges, sharp pencils, stored flat and dry

essays.stem: Why is it important to work only from the latest revision of a drawing? What could go wrong if an old copy is used?
essays.modelAnswer: Drawings are often changed during a job, because the customer asks for changes, the building design changes, or a mistake is found. Each change is given a new revision letter or number in the title block, with a short note saying what was changed. If I work from an old copy, I may fit outlets, switches or lights in the wrong places, run cables along a route that is now blocked, or use the wrong cable or breaker size. Work must then be taken out and done again, which wastes time and materials and costs money. It can also be unsafe if the circuits are not wired as the designer intended. Old copies should be marked out of date or taken off site.
markingPoints: Drawings change during a job for good reasons
Each change has a revision letter or number in the title block
Old copies lead to wrong positions, routes or sizes
Rework wastes time, materials and money
Can be unsafe; old copies must be marked or removed

essays.stem: Describe the main types of line used on drawings, and say what each one shows.
essays.modelAnswer: A thick continuous line is used for outlines and edges that you can see, such as the walls of a room. A thin continuous line is used for dimension lines, projection (extension) lines and hatching. A thin dashed line shows edges that are hidden from that view. On electrical layout drawings, a dashed or curved line is often used to show which switch controls which light; it does not show the real cable route. A thin chain line, made of long and short dashes, shows the centre lines of circles and holes. Dimension lines have arrowheads or ticks at each end, with the size written above the line. Using the right type of line makes a drawing quick and easy to read.
markingPoints: Thick continuous line for visible outlines
Thin continuous lines for dimensions and projection lines
Dashed line for hidden detail
Dashed switch-to-light line on electrical layouts shows control, not route
Chain line for centre lines

essays.stem: Compare drawing by hand with drawing on a computer (CAD) for electrical drawings. Give two good points of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Drawing by hand needs only paper, pencils and simple instruments, so it is cheap and can be done anywhere, even on a site with no power. It is good for quick sketches, and it helps a trainee learn how a drawing is built up. However, changes take time, because lines must be rubbed out and drawn again. Drawing with CAD needs a computer, software and training. Its good points are that it is very accurate and that changes are quick to make. Symbols can be kept in a library and used again and again, and drawings can be saved, printed at any scale and sent by email. Many offices now use CAD, but an electrician still needs to read drawings and sketch by hand on site.
markingPoints: Hand: cheap and can be done anywhere
Hand: good for quick sketches and learning
CAD: accurate, with quick changes
CAD: symbol libraries, saving, printing at any scale and sharing
Notes a weakness of each or gives a balanced conclusion

practical1.title: Measure rooms at the Centre and draw their electrical layouts to scale
practical1.brief: The assessor gives each member one room or area at the Centre, for example a classroom, office, store or workshop bay. Measure your room with the tape and make a freehand sketch with all the sizes, including doors and windows. Then draw a layout of your room at 1:50 on an A3 sheet, with a border and a title block, showing the lights, switches, outlets and fixed equipment that are there now, in the right places. Show which switch controls which light. As a group, first agree one legend of symbols and one title block layout for everyone to use. Each member draws their own sheet and checks one other member's sheet before hand-in. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every drawing is finished and checked.
materials: Clipboard, sketch paper and pencils (2H and HB)
A3 drawing paper and masking tape
Drawing board with T-square and set squares, or a drawing table
Scale rule, eraser and electrical symbol template
List of rooms from the assessor
photos: Each member measuring their room, with the tape in view
Each freehand sketch with the sizes written on it
The group's agreed legend of symbols
Each layout drawing at the light guide-line stage
Each finished layout drawing with title block and legend
checklist: Measured the room accurately and recorded all sizes on a sketch
Used the 1:50 scale correctly with a scale rule
Drew walls, doors and windows to scale with neat and correct line types
Used the correct symbol for each light, switch and outlet, in the right place
Showed which switch controls which light
Completed the title block (title, scale, date, drawn by, drawing number) and legend
Lettering clear and even; drawing clean and neat
Checked another member's drawing and noted any errors politely
safety: Watch for trip hazards and wet floors when measuring; do not enter a workshop bay while machines are running
Do not open any board, outlet or switch to look inside; draw only what can be seen
Use a stepladder only with the assessor's permission, and never stand on the top step
Keep drawing instruments and sharp pencils in their case when they are not in use

practical2.title: Draw circuit and wiring diagrams from a wired training board
practical2.brief: The assessor provides a training board that is already wired and is not connected to any supply. It has a one-way lighting circuit, a two-way lighting circuit, a lighting circuit with two-way and intermediate switches, and a radial outlet circuit, all fed from a small distribution board. The accessories have clear covers, or the assessor has removed their fronts, so that every terminal can be seen without touching. Each member takes one circuit; in a group of five, one member draws a single-line diagram of the distribution board instead. Follow your circuit from accessory to accessory by eye and draw: (1) a circuit diagram using the agreed symbols, and (2) a wiring diagram that shows each terminal and the conductor connected to it. Then swap drawings with another member, who checks yours against the board. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Wired training board with lighting and outlet circuits (not connected to any supply), terminals visible
Drawing instruments, scale rule, pencils and eraser
Electrical symbol template and the agreed legend
photos: The training board, showing the circuits to be drawn
Each member's rough sketch made while following their circuit
The single-line diagram of the distribution board (where drawn)
Members checking a drawing against the board
checklist: Followed the circuit correctly from the distribution board to every accessory
Used the agreed symbols and drew straight horizontal and vertical lines
Showed the switch in the line conductor and the protective device in the circuit
Showed junction dots where conductors join and labelled L, N and E
Wiring diagram shows each terminal and the conductor connected to it
Completed a title, legend and drawing number on each sheet
Checked another member's drawing against the board and reported any errors
Did not touch any terminal or remove any cover
safety: The training board must not be connected to any supply: do not plug it in or switch it on
Do not touch terminals or remove covers; look only
Keep the area around the board clear so that nobody trips
Follow the Centre's rules for the training bay
